claim: Rodeh (2006, IBM Research Report H-0245) splits each full index node on the way down to a leaf: 'On the way down to a leaf each full index node is split' (section 5.3).
handles: proactive split on the way down

claim: Rodeh (2006) fixes each node with a minimal amount of keys on the way up: 'each node with a minimal amount of keys is fixed' (section 5.5).
Rodeh (2006, self-reported): 'The number of modified disk-pages can be 2 x tree-depth' with 3 memory pages at worst (section 5.6, paper line 332).
Rodeh (2006) clones a tree by copying its root-node into a new root and incrementing the free-space counters for each child of the root (section 6.1).
Rodeh (2006) describes the first write to a shared page as one that 'splits C into two versions' (section 6.3).

Rodeh (2006, self-reported): ten tasks reached a speedup of about x6 over one task on a disk-bound lookup load, against an ideal baseline computed from the disk rate and not another tree (16-byte entries, 4 KB pages, about 64,000 leaves and 4 levels, one machine with a disk array).
Rodeh (2006, self-reported): with 2 clones throughput was 1303, 733, 394, 350 ops/s against 1307, 763, 407, 359 ops/s without clones (Table 8).
Rodeh (2006, self-reported): a checkpoint shows 'between 3% and 10% degradation' (section 8.5).
Rodeh (2006, self-reported): node bounds are [b, 2b+1] then 'expanded to [b, 3b]', and 'The average capacity of a node is around 2b'.
Rodeh (2006, self-reported): under an append-only workload both trees, T235 and T150, had an average occupancy of 50%, which the paper says is 'caused by the append-only workload'.
Rodeh (2006) assumes that every tree modification has to exclusively lock the root and one of its children, which 'was not a problem' because the root and children are cached (paper line 541).
Driscoll et al. (1989) describe node copying: 'If there is no space in a predecessor ... the predecessor, too, must be copied' (alt.txt lines 360-364).

Driscoll et al. (1989) prove, with no measurement, an 'amortized space cost of 0(1) per update step and a constant factor in the amortized time' for nodes of constant in-degree (alt.txt lines 187-190).
note: OCR text (alt.txt): the quoted figure is written 0(1) in the extraction, as the input has it; read as O(1) by context, not by the glyph.

claim: Driscoll et al. (1989) state that copying the entire access path 'requires O(1ogn) space and time in the worst case per insertion or deletion', so their method 'saves a logarithmic factor in space' (alt.txt lines 1446-1449).
note: OCR text (alt.txt); the extraction reads O(1ogn) for O(log n), so the words were checked, not the glyphs.

claim: Becker et al. (1996) state, as a worst-case bound and not a measurement, that the number of block accesses and modifications for the (i+1)-th update operation is 5 x log_d m_i (Theorem 3, paper line 371).
Becker et al. (1996) state that the worst-case amortized space cost per update operation, S = S_dat + S_dir, is O(1) if d >= 2 (Theorem 4, paper line 437).
Becker et al. (1996) bound the amortized data-block space cost per update by '<= 2 x k x d / (e x d + 1)' (inequality 3, paper lines 418-421).
Becker et al. (1996) describe a version split: 'The structural modification after a block overflow copies the block and removes all but the current entries from the copy' (paper lines 162-164).
Becker et al. (1996) state the strong version condition: after a version split 'the number of current entries ... must be in the range from (1 + e) x d to (k - e) x d' (paper lines 178-179).
Becker et al. (1996) state the weak version underflow: 'weak version underflow occurs if an entry is deleted in a block with exactly d current entries' (paper line 153).
Becker et al. (1996) give the inequality '(k - e) x d + 1 >= 2 x (1 + e) x d' (paper line 375) and, for B-trees, state that 'the fraction guaranteed in a new node is 0.5' (paper line 383).

Gray and Graefe (1997) define IndexPageBenefit/Cost = IndexPageUtility / IndexPageAccessCost, with IndexPageUtility = log2(EntriesPerPage) (paper line 288) and IndexPageAccessCost = Disk Latency + PageSize / DiskTransferRate (paper line 324).

Gray and Graefe (1997) calculate, and do not measure, IndexPageBenefit/Cost of 0.60 at 2 KB, 0.68 at 4 KB, 0.75 at 8 KB, 0.78 at 16 KB (541 entries), 0.76 at 32 KB, 0.68 at 64 KB and 0.53 at 128 KB, for 20-byte entries, 70% full, 10 ms latency and 10 MB/s (Table 6, paper lines 346-368).
Gray and Graefe (1997) state that 'index page sizes in the range of 8 KB to 32 KB are preferable' (paper line 306).
Chu (2011, LMDB design paper) allows only one writer at a time: 'the MDB library allows only one writer at a time' (paper line 240).
Chu (2011, LMDB design paper) states that readers are not blocked: 'nothing that can block the operation of readers' (paper line 255).
Chu (2011, LMDB design paper) writes with copy-on-write: 'whenever a page is to be written, a copy is made and the copy is modified instead of the original' (paper line 258).

Chu (2011, LMDB design paper) states that a reader holding an old snapshot for a long time only blocks page reclaiming: 'The only consequence of a reader holding onto an old snapshot for a long time is that page reclaiming cannot be done' (paper lines 268-270).

Chu (2011, LMDB design paper, self-reported): 16 concurrent searches took 0m12.023s on back-mdb against 3m04.464s on back-hdb (Table 3, paper lines 346-352), on OpenLDAP search of a fully cached database of the authors' test set.
note: Table 3 row labels were garbled in text extraction; the input takes the smaller time as back-mdb and marks that uncertain.

claim: Chu (2011, LMDB design paper, self-reported) reports 37% as much RAM as back-hdb (paper line 341).
Chu (2011, LMDB design paper, self-reported): 'Write performance has been traded for read performance' (paper line 420).
Chu (2011, LMDB design paper, self-reported): without page reuse the database occupied 1027 pages but only 10 pages held current data, so over 99% of the space was wasted (paper line 200).
Chu (2011, LMDB design paper, self-reported): with garbage collection the database used 'twice as much disk space as the actual data occupies' (paper lines 161-166).
note: The paper's I/O figure in the same passage lost its symbol in text extraction and is not recorded here.

claim: Safavi and Seybold (2023) state that classic B-trees 'guarantee that every block, beside the root, has a load-factor of at least 1/2' (paper lines 69-77).
Safavi and Seybold (2023) state that the B*-tree variant guarantees a load-factor of at least 2/3 through an overflow strategy 'that shares keys among the two neighboring nodes' (paper lines 69-77).

Safavi and Seybold (2023), stating Yao's analysis, give an expected asymptotic load-factor under random-order insertion of ln(2), about 69%, for B-trees and 2 ln(3/2), about 81%, for B*-trees (paper lines 69-77).
note: Second-hand: Safavi and Seybold's statement of Yao 1978, which was not opened (see x38-0343).

claim: Safavi and Seybold (2023) state that for general workloads 'maintaining higher load-factors (with even wider overflow strategies) further increases the write-bounds of updates' (paper lines 69-77).

Comer (1979) quotes the definition by Knuth, 'a B*-tree to be a B-tree in which each node is at least 2/3 full', and states 'This scheme guarantees that storage utilization is at least 66%' (paper lines 484-495).
Comer (1979) states that B+-trees give 'guaranteed storage utilization of 50%' (paper line 781).
Comer (1979) states that 'increasing storage utilization has the side effect of speeding up the search since the height of the resulting tree is smaller' (paper lines 497-501).

Comer (1979) describes B*-tree redistribution: 'instead of splitting a node as soon as it fills up, keys could merely be distributed into a neighboring node, splitting only when two neighbors fill' (paper lines 484-490).
Comer (1979) states that a split key is 'promoted to the parent node where it serves as a separator' and that 'splitting propagates all the way' to the root in the worst case (paper lines 297-311).
Comer (1979) states that underflow is handled by redistribution among two neighbours (paper lines 353-354).

Yao (1978), as reported by Comer (1979), analysed 2-3 trees built from uniformly distributed keys and extended the analysis to higher-order B-trees, where 'the expected storage utilization is ln 2 = 69%' (Comer's text, paper lines 731-741).
Bayer and Schkolnick (1977), as reported by Comer (1979), state that 'readers lock at most two nodes at any time' (paper lines 739-741).

Comer (1979) reports top-down splitting suggested in [GUIB78] in which 'only one pair of nodes will ever be locked at a given time', at 'a slight decrease in storage utilization' (paper lines 786-800).
The LMDB reference documentation (Chu, Symas) states that data pages use copy-on-write so that 'no active data pages are ever overwritten' (paper line 74).
The LMDB reference documentation states that 'only one write transaction may be active at a time, which guarantees that writers can never deadlock' (paper line 74).
The LMDB reference documentation states that 'readers run with no locks; writers cannot block readers, and readers don't block writers' (paper line 74).
The LMDB reference documentation states that LMDB 'tracks free pages within the database and re-uses them for new write operations' (paper line 75).
The LMDB reference documentation warns that 'Read transactions prevent reuse of pages freed by newer write transactions, thus the database can grow quickly' (paper line 119).
